en: The word Halloween is short for All Hallows' Eve. Hallow is an old English word for saint, so Halloween simply means the evening before All Saints' Day, which is celebrated on the first of November.

Many historians think some Halloween customs go back to Samhain, an ancient Celtic festival at the end of the harvest, when people believed the boundary with the world of the dead grew thin. Others stress its Christian roots.

In the seven hundreds, Pope Gregory the Third dedicated a chapel in Rome to all the saints on the first of November. The feast later spread across the whole Church, and the night before it became All Hallows' Eve.

Trick or treat may have a Christian ancestor called souling. In medieval England, poor people and children went from door to door around All Souls' Day, offering prayers for the dead in exchange for small cakes called soul cakes.

hook.en: Halloween began as the eve of a Christian feast.

en: Reformation Day is celebrated on the thirty first of October. It remembers the day in fifteen seventeen when the monk Martin Luther sent his Ninety-Five Theses, a list of arguments against the sale of indulgences, to his archbishop.

Indulgences were documents promising less punishment for sins after death. A preacher named Johann Tetzel was famous for selling them in Germany, and a saying was linked to him: as soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.

The famous image of Luther hammering his theses onto the church door in Wittenberg comes from later accounts. In the nineteen sixties, a historian argued it never happened, and scholars still debate it. What is certain is that Luther mailed them.

Thanks to the new printing press, Luther's ideas spread across Germany in just a few weeks. Later, while hiding in Wartburg Castle, he translated the whole New Testament into German in only about eleven weeks.

hook.en: Luther may never have nailed his theses to a door.

en: All Saints' Day is celebrated on the first of November by Catholics and many Protestants. In France, Italy, Spain, Poland and other countries it is a public holiday, and families visit cemeteries and decorate graves with flowers.
In Poland, cemeteries glow on All Saints' Day. Millions of people light candles in little glass lanterns on the graves, and whole hillsides of tombs shine with thousands of tiny flames after dark.

The feast is not only for famous saints who have their own day. It honors all the faithful in heaven, known and unknown, including ordinary people whose holiness was never officially recognized by any church.
Orthodox Christians also have a feast of All Saints, but on a different day. They celebrate it on the first Sunday after Pentecost, so its date changes every year, just like Easter.

hook.en: All Saints' Day honors saints nobody has ever heard of.

paintings: Fra Angelico Forerunners of Christ with Saints and Martyrs

en: The Bible says Noah was six hundred years old when the flood began, and lived three hundred and fifty more years after it. In the whole Bible, only Methuselah and Jared are said to have lived longer.
Noah did not take just two of every animal. Genesis says that for the clean animals, the ones later used for sacrifice, he was told to take seven pairs. Only the other animals came in a single pair.

Genesis gives the size of the ark: three hundred cubits long. A cubit was about forty five centimeters, the length of a forearm. That makes the ark around one hundred and thirty five meters long, longer than an American football field.

The ark is not the only ancient flood story. The Epic of Gilgamesh, from Mesopotamia, tells of a man who builds a huge boat, saves animals, and sends out birds to find dry land. Scholars think it is older than the written Genesis.

hook.en: Noah's Ark was longer than a football field.

paintings: Jacopo Bassano animals entering the Ark

en: All Souls' Day falls on the second of November. While All Saints' Day celebrates those already in heaven, this day is for praying for all the faithful who have died, and remembering family members who are gone.

In Mexico, these days are part of the Day of the Dead. Families build colorful altars with photos, candles, marigold flowers and the favorite foods of loved ones who have died, mixing old local traditions with Catholic feasts.

The feast was started around the year nine hundred and ninety eight by Odilo, the abbot of the great monastery of Cluny in France. He asked his monks to pray for all the dead on that day, and the custom spread across Europe.

In parts of Europe, people once left a lit candle in the window on All Souls' night. In some places church bells rang for hours, and soul cakes were given to the poor, who promised to pray for the dead in return.

hook.en: All Souls' Day was started by a medieval monk.

en: The Dead Sea Scrolls include some of the oldest known copies of the Bible, written more than two thousand years ago. Every book of the Hebrew Bible appears among them, except one, the Book of Esther.

They were hidden in eleven caves near Qumran, close to the Dead Sea. Scholars count around nine hundred manuscripts, but most survive only as fragments, some smaller than a postage stamp, like a giant puzzle with missing pieces.

Around nineteen forty seven, a young Bedouin shepherd was searching for a lost goat. He threw a stone into a cave and heard pottery break. Inside were clay jars holding ancient scrolls, and the first ones were sold for very little money.

One scroll is unlike all the others. The Copper Scroll is engraved on metal, and it lists dozens of hiding places of gold and silver. Treasure hunters have searched for decades, but nobody has ever found any of it.

hook.en: A shepherd chasing a lost goat found them.

en: Moses was born when Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into the Nile. His mother hid him for three months, then put him in a basket covered with tar and left it among the reeds of the river.
Moses did not feel ready to lead. At the burning bush, he told God he was slow of speech and begged him to send someone else. So God chose his older brother Aaron to speak for him.

The basket was found by the daughter of Pharaoh herself, who adopted the crying baby. Even better, his own mother was secretly hired to nurse him. So the future leader of the Hebrews grew up in the Egyptian royal palace.

Moses never entered the promised land. After forty years in the desert, he climbed Mount Nebo and saw it from far away. He died there at one hundred and twenty, and the Bible says nobody knows where his grave is.

hook.en: Moses grew up as a prince of Egypt.

en: In April twenty nineteen, a fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame. The roof frame used so much old oak that it was nicknamed the forest. After a huge restoration, the cathedral reopened in December twenty twenty four.
Notre-Dame keeps a relic that tradition calls the crown of thorns of Jesus. On the night of the fire, a priest and firefighters went into the burning cathedral and carried it out to safety.

The first stone of Notre-Dame was laid in eleven sixty three, and the main work only ended around thirteen forty five. The workers who started it never saw it finished, and neither did their children or grandchildren.

In the eighteen hundreds, Notre-Dame was falling apart and some wanted it torn down. The novel by Victor Hugo, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, made it famous again and helped save it with a big restoration.

hook.en: Notre-Dame took almost two hundred years to build.

en: Genesis says a river flowed out of Eden and split into four. Two of those rivers still have the same names, the Tigris and the Euphrates, in modern Iraq. But the garden itself has never been found.
Eden had two special trees, not one. Besides the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, there was the tree of life. After Adam and Eve left, cherubim and a flaming sword guarded the way to it.

Genesis only says the fruit of the tree. The apple came later, in Western Europe, maybe because in Latin the word malum means both evil and apple. Some Jewish traditions said it was a fig, grapes, or even wheat.

The name Eden is linked to a Hebrew word meaning delight. The Greek translation of the Bible called the garden paradeisos, a Persian word for a walled royal park. That is where our word paradise comes from.

hook.en: The Bible never says the forbidden fruit was an apple.

en: The Knights Templar began around eleven nineteen in Jerusalem, with only a handful of knights. They protected Christian pilgrims on the roads to the Holy Land, and they took vows like monks while also being trained warriors.

Their name comes from their first home. The King of Jerusalem gave them part of his palace on the Temple Mount, linked to the ancient Temple of Solomon. So they became the Knights of the Temple, the Templars.

On Friday the thirteenth of October, thirteen oh seven, King Philip the Fourth of France, who owed them a fortune, had Templars across his kingdom arrested at dawn. Many link this to the unlucky Friday the thirteenth, but historians doubt it.

The Templars were some of the first international bankers. A pilgrim could leave money with them in Europe, get a written note, and collect the money again in the Holy Land, safe from robbers on the road.

hook.en: The Templars were arrested on Friday the thirteenth.

en: People have lived in Jerusalem for more than five thousand years. For Christians, it is where Jesus was crucified and, according to the Gospels, rose again. It is also a holy city for Jews and Muslims.

The Old City is tiny, less than one square kilometer. Its walls, built in the fifteen hundreds by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, have several gates, and one of them, the Golden Gate, has been sealed for centuries.

According to the historian Eric Cline, Jerusalem has been attacked fifty two times, captured and recaptured forty four times, besieged twenty three times, and destroyed twice. Few cities on Earth have been fought over so often.
Many medieval maps put Jerusalem at the exact center of the world. On the famous Hereford map in England, the earth is a circle with the holy city in the middle, as the spiritual heart of the world.

hook.en: Jerusalem has been attacked more than fifty times.

en: David was the youngest of eight brothers and a shepherd. When the prophet Samuel came to choose a king among the sons of Jesse, David was not even invited. He had to be called in from the fields.
David first came to King Saul's court as a musician, playing the lyre to calm the troubled king. Later Saul became so jealous of him that he tried to kill him, even throwing a spear at him.
David was a poet as much as a warrior. In the Hebrew Bible, seventy three of the one hundred and fifty Psalms carry his name, including Psalm twenty three, which begins, the Lord is my shepherd.

For a long time, some scholars doubted David even existed. Then in nineteen ninety three, archaeologists found a stone inscription mentioning the House of David. It is the oldest known mention of David outside the Bible.

hook.en: David is credited with writing seventy three Psalms.

paintings: Honthorst King David playing the harp
Caravaggio David with the Head of Goliath

en: The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth more than four meters long, showing the faint image of a crucified man. Many Christians believe it is the burial cloth of Jesus. It is kept in Turin, Italy, and rarely shown.

In nineteen eighty eight, three laboratories carbon dated the cloth to the Middle Ages, between about twelve sixty and thirteen ninety. Some researchers think the sample came from a repaired corner, so the debate goes on.

In eighteen ninety eight, a lawyer named Secondo Pia took the first photo of the shroud. On his glass negative, the face suddenly looked clear and lifelike, because the image on the cloth itself behaves like a photographic negative.

In fifteen thirty two, the shroud almost burned in a chapel fire in France. Melted silver from its box dripped onto the folded cloth and burned holes in it. Nuns sewed patches over them, and the marks are still visible.

hook.en: The Shroud of Turin works like a photographic negative.

paintings: Shroud of Turin negative Secondo Pia

en: Judas was one of the twelve apostles, and the Gospel of John says he kept the group's money bag. John even accuses him of stealing from it. So Jesus had trusted him with the money of the whole group.
Judas gave the soldiers a secret signal: the man he kissed was the one to arrest. That night in the garden of Gethsemane, he greeted Jesus with a kiss, and that kiss became a symbol of betrayal.

Matthew says Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver, and that amount was not random. In the Book of Exodus, thirty shekels of silver is the price paid when an ox kills a slave. Jesus was sold for the price of a slave.
Judas later regretted it and threw the silver back into the Temple. The priests would not keep blood money, so they bought a potter's field to bury foreigners. It became known as the Field of Blood.

hook.en: Judas betrayed Jesus for the price of a slave.

en: The Sistine Chapel is where cardinals are locked in to elect a new pope. Black smoke from its chimney means no pope yet. White smoke tells the waiting crowd that a new pope has been chosen.

Michelangelo painted the ceiling from fifteen oh eight to fifteen twelve, with more than three hundred figures. Despite the legend, he did not lie on his back. He stood on a platform he designed, his head bent backward.

Michelangelo saw himself as a sculptor, not a painter, but Pope Julius the Second insisted. He even wrote a poem complaining about the job, with his beard pointing to heaven, paint dripping on his face, and his body bent like a bow.

Years later, Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment behind the altar, full of nude figures that shocked church leaders. After his death, another painter covered them with cloth, and was mocked as the breeches maker.

hook.en: Michelangelo did not want to paint the Sistine Chapel.

en: The last book of the Bible is Revelation, not Revelations. Its Greek title is Apokalypsis, meaning an unveiling. That is where our word apocalypse comes from, even though it did not originally mean the end of the world.

Revelation loves the number seven: seven churches, seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, seven stars. For ancient readers seven meant completeness, so many scholars think the numbers are symbols, not exact counts.

The author, John, says he saw his visions on Patmos, a small Greek island, because of his witness to Jesus. Early Christians said a Roman emperor had exiled him there. A cave on Patmos is still visited as the place of his visions.

Revelation was one of the last books accepted into the Bible, and the Eastern churches debated it for centuries. Even today, it is the only New Testament book never read aloud in the main Orthodox liturgy.

hook.en: The Book of Revelation was written in exile.

en: Flood stories appear in many ancient cultures, from Mesopotamia and Greece to India and the Americas. In the Greek myth, a man named Deucalion and his wife survive the flood inside a wooden chest.
Noah sent out a raven, then a dove that came back with nothing. The second time, the dove returned with a fresh olive leaf in its beak, and that image became a worldwide symbol of peace.

The forty days of rain were only the beginning. Genesis says the waters covered the earth for one hundred and fifty days, and counting the dates in the text, Noah stayed in the ark for about a full year.
After the flood, Genesis says God put a rainbow in the clouds as a promise never to flood the earth again. The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia.

hook.en: The flood lasted much longer than forty days.

paintings: Thomas Cole Subsiding of the Waters of the Deluge

en: Mary Magdalene probably came from Magdala, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke says she was one of several women who followed Jesus and paid for his mission with their own money.
All four Gospels place Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb on Easter morning. In John, she is the very first to see Jesus risen, so early Christians called her the apostle to the apostles.

The prostitute idea is not in the Bible. It comes from a sermon by Pope Gregory the Great in five ninety one, which mixed her up with other women. In twenty sixteen, the Catholic Church gave her a full feast day.

A French legend says Mary Magdalene sailed to Provence and lived her last years in a cave. A basilica in Saint-Maximin claims to hold her skull, still carried through the streets every year in a golden case.

hook.en: The Bible never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute.

en: The Hebrew word behind these unicorns is reem, a strong wild animal with powerful horns that nobody could tame. In the Book of Job, God asks if the reem would ever agree to work for a farmer.

Many scholars think the reem was the aurochs, a giant wild ox almost two meters tall at the shoulder. It once roamed the Middle East and Europe, and the last one died in a Polish forest in sixteen twenty seven.

Greek translators of the Bible chose monokeros, meaning one horn, and Latin used unicornis. So the King James Bible of sixteen eleven said unicorn, nine times. Most modern Bibles now just say wild ox.
In the Middle Ages, the unicorn became a symbol of Christ. Unicorn horns were sold as powerful medicine, but most of them were actually tusks from the narwhal, a whale of the Arctic.

hook.en: The King James Bible mentions unicorns nine times.

en: Bethlehem is about ten kilometers south of Jerusalem. Long before Jesus, it was famous as the hometown of King David, which is why the Gospels call it the city of David.
The Church of the Nativity is entered through the Door of Humility, a doorway so low that most adults must bend down. It was probably made small to stop people riding in on horses.
In Hebrew, Bethlehem is Beit Lechem, meaning house of bread. And in the Gospel of John, Jesus calls himself the bread of life. So the bread of life was born in the house of bread.

A silver star in a cave under the church marks the traditional birthplace of Jesus. In eighteen forty seven the star was stolen, and the quarrel over replacing it added to the tensions before the Crimean War.

hook.en: Bethlehem's name means house of bread.

en: Before Samson was born, an angel said he would be a Nazirite, set apart for God. That meant no wine, never touching a dead body, and never cutting his hair. His strength was tied to that promise.

The Philistine leaders each offered Delilah eleven hundred pieces of silver to find the secret of his strength. Samson lied to her three times. The fourth time he told the truth, and his head was shaved while he slept.
The Book of Judges says a young lion came roaring at Samson. With no weapon at all, he tore it apart like a young goat. Later he found bees and honey inside its body, and turned it into a riddle.
Blinded and chained, Samson was brought into a Philistine temple to entertain a crowd. He prayed for strength one last time, pushed apart the two middle pillars, and brought the whole temple down.

hook.en: Samson once killed a lion with his bare hands.

en: The Ark of the Covenant was a wooden chest covered in gold, a little over one meter long. It held the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, and Hebrews adds a jar of manna and the staff of Aaron.
The Ark was never carried by hand. Golden poles went through rings on its sides, and priests carried it on their shoulders. The Bible says those poles must never be taken out.
Once, the Ark was moved on a cart and the oxen stumbled. A man named Uzzah reached out to steady it with his hand, and the Bible says he died on the spot. Even King David was afraid of it after that.

Nobody knows where the Ark went. It vanishes from the Bible around the fall of Jerusalem. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church says it is in a chapel in Aksum, guarded by one monk who may never show it to anyone.

hook.en: Touching the Ark of the Covenant could be deadly.

title.en: the parting of the Red Sea

en: When the Israelites left Egypt, Pharaoh changed his mind and chased them with six hundred of his best chariots. Trapped against the sea, the people panicked, but Moses told them to stand still and watch.
The sea did not open in an instant. Exodus says a strong east wind blew all night and made the sea dry land, with the water like a wall on each side. In the morning, it came back over the chariots.

In Hebrew, it is called yam suph, which many scholars translate as sea of reeds. The name Red Sea came from the Greek translation. Since reeds need fresh water, some think the crossing was at a marshy lake.

In twenty ten, scientists used computer models to show that a strong all night wind could push water back and open a dry path in a shallow lagoon of the Nile delta. For believers, the timing is the miracle.

hook.en: The Hebrew Bible may not say Red Sea at all.

paintings: Crossing of the Red Sea painting

en: Augustine was born in three fifty four in North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His mother Monica was a devoted Christian, but his father was not, and young Augustine became a brilliant teacher of public speaking.

His book Confessions is often called the first real autobiography in the West. He even confesses stealing pears from a neighbor's tree as a teenager, not because he was hungry, but for the thrill of it.
Before his conversion, Augustine wanted to change but kept delaying. In Confessions he admits praying, give me chastity and self control, but not yet. He was afraid God would answer him too quickly.

In a garden in Milan, Augustine heard a child singing, take up and read. He opened Paul's letters at random, read a verse about leaving his old life, and changed. He became one of the greatest thinkers in Christian history.

hook.en: Saint Augustine once prayed, make me pure, but not yet.

paintings: Botticelli Saint Augustine in his study

en: Genesis says that after the flood, everyone spoke one language. People decided to build a city with a tower reaching to the heavens, to make a name for themselves, using baked bricks and tar instead of stone.
In the story, God confuses their language so they can no longer understand each other, and they scatter across the earth. Genesis links the name Babel to a Hebrew word meaning to confuse.

Many historians think the story was inspired by the ziggurats of Mesopotamia, huge stepped temple towers. In Babylon stood one called Etemenanki, the temple of the foundation of heaven and earth, about ninety meters tall.

The famous painting of the tower by Pieter Bruegel the Elder makes it look like the Roman Colosseum. Today, many people say a European Parliament building in Strasbourg looks just like Bruegel's unfinished tower.

hook.en: Babel may have been a real Babylonian tower.

en: Hagia Sophia means holy wisdom in Greek, not Saint Sophia. It was built in Constantinople, today's Istanbul, by the emperor Justinian, and it took less than six years, finishing in the year five thirty seven.
Its giant dome seems to float on a ring of forty windows. But earthquakes were a problem, and only about twenty years after it was finished, the first dome collapsed and had to be rebuilt.
For almost a thousand years, Hagia Sophia was the largest cathedral in the world. It only lost that title in the fifteen hundreds, when the cathedral of Seville in Spain was finally completed.

In fourteen fifty three, the Ottomans conquered the city and turned Hagia Sophia into a mosque. In nineteen thirty four it became a museum, and in twenty twenty it became a mosque again, still open to visitors.

hook.en: For almost a thousand years, no cathedral was bigger.

en: Before he followed Jesus, Paul, then called Saul, persecuted Christians. The Book of Acts says he guarded the coats of the men who stoned Stephen, the first Christian martyr, and approved of his death.
Paul was a tentmaker by trade. Even while preaching, he often worked with his own hands to pay his way, so that nobody could say he was preaching for money.

Thirteen of the twenty seven books of the New Testament are letters carrying the name of Paul. Scholars debate whether he wrote all of them himself, but his letters are among the oldest Christian writings we have.

Paul wrote that he was shipwrecked three times, beaten with rods three times, and stoned once, and that was before his famous shipwreck on Malta. Tradition says he was finally beheaded in Rome under the emperor Nero.

hook.en: Paul's name is on almost half the New Testament.

en: The Nephilim appear in just a few verses of Genesis, right before the story of the flood. They are called the mighty men of old, men of renown, and their name is often translated as giants.
Genesis says they appeared when the sons of God took human wives. Some ancient writers said these sons of God were fallen angels, while others think they were simply men from the family of Seth.

The Nephilim show up again after the flood. In the Book of Numbers, spies sent into Canaan say they saw them, and that next to them, we were like grasshoppers. That puzzle has fascinated readers for thousands of years.
The Book of Enoch, an ancient Jewish text left out of most Bibles, tells a much longer story. It says fallen angels taught humans secret arts, and their giant children brought chaos to the earth.

hook.en: The Bible mentions giants before and after the flood.

en: God told Jonah to go to Nineveh, a great city of the Assyrians, Israel's enemies. Instead, Jonah boarded a ship sailing the other way, toward Tarshish, which many think was in Spain.
A terrible storm hit the ship. The sailors cast lots to find who was to blame, and the lot fell on Jonah. He told them to throw him overboard, and as soon as they did, the sea became calm.

The Hebrew text says a great fish swallowed Jonah, and he stayed inside three days and three nights. The Greek word later used by Matthew means sea monster. The whale mostly comes from old English translations.
When Jonah finally preached in Nineveh, the whole city repented, even the king. Jonah was angry that God spared them, and the book ends with God asking him a question that Jonah never answers.

hook.en: The Book of Jonah never says it was a whale.

paintings: Pieter Lastman Jonah and the Whale

en: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from about the year twenty six to thirty six. Roman and Jewish writers describe him as harsh and stubborn, a man who often offended the people he ruled.
For a long time, there was no proof of Pilate outside written texts. Then in nineteen sixty one, archaeologists in Caesarea found a stone carved with his name and title, now called the Pilate Stone.

In the Gospels, Pilate washes his hands and says he is innocent of the blood of Jesus. Because of this, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors both Pilate and his wife as saints, believing he later became a Christian.

Matthew says that during the trial, Pilate's wife sent him an urgent message. She had suffered much in a dream because of Jesus, and she warned her husband to have nothing to do with that righteous man.

hook.en: One church honors Pontius Pilate as a saint.

en: Under Rome lie dozens of catacombs, underground tunnels dug into soft volcanic rock. Together they stretch for well over one hundred kilometers, on several levels, some more than twenty meters deep.
Their walls are lined with shelves cut into the rock, where bodies were wrapped in cloth and sealed in. Hundreds of thousands of people may have been buried there, many of them poor Christians.

Movies show Christians hiding in the catacombs from Roman persecution, but historians say they were mainly cemeteries. Roman law protected burial places, and Christians went there to bury and remember their dead, not to live in secret.

The catacombs hold some of the oldest Christian art in the world. Early believers painted the Good Shepherd, Jonah and the whale, and the fish symbol on their walls, long before the first big churches.

hook.en: Early Christians did not hide in the catacombs.

en: When Solomon became king, the Bible says God offered him anything he wanted. Instead of riches or a long life, he asked for wisdom to rule well, and God was so pleased that he gave him riches and honor too.
Solomon built the first Temple in Jerusalem. The Bible says no hammer, axe or iron tool was heard at the site, because the stones were cut and prepared at the quarry before being brought there.

The First Book of Kings says Solomon had seven hundred wives who were princesses, and three hundred concubines. Many were foreign brides that sealed alliances, and the Bible says they turned his heart to other gods.

The Bible says Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, wrote more than a thousand songs, and could teach about trees, animals, birds and fish. Tradition links him to Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs.

hook.en: King Solomon had seven hundred wives.

paintings: Poynter Visit of the Queen of Sheba to King Solomon

en: Methuselah is the oldest person in the Bible. Genesis says he lived nine hundred and sixty nine years, which is why people still say as old as Methuselah about something extremely old.
Methuselah came from a remarkable family. His father was Enoch, who walked with God and then was no more, because God took him. And his grandson was Noah, the builder of the ark.
If you add up the ages given in Genesis, Methuselah died in the very same year the great flood began. Some Jewish traditions even say the flood was delayed seven days so he could be mourned.

A bristlecone pine in the White Mountains of California is nicknamed Methuselah. It is more than four thousand eight hundred years old, one of the oldest known trees, and its exact location is kept secret.

hook.en: Methuselah died in the year of the flood.

en: Many of the most famous Gospel stories happen around this lake. It is where Jesus called fishermen like Peter and Andrew, calmed a storm, and, according to the Gospels, walked on the water.

In nineteen eighty six, during a drought, two brothers found an ancient fishing boat in the mud of the shore. It dates from around the time of Jesus, and it is now shown in a museum as the Jesus Boat.
Despite its name, the Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake, only about twenty one kilometers long. It lies about two hundred meters below sea level, making it the lowest freshwater lake on Earth.
Its sudden storms are real. Cool winds rush down from the hills into the low basin, and the calm water can turn into dangerous waves in minutes, just like in the Gospel stories.

hook.en: The Sea of Galilee is actually a lake.

paintings: Rembrandt Storm on the Sea of Galilee

en: Joan was a peasant girl from a village in eastern France. At about thirteen, she said she began hearing the voices of saints, who later told her to help the French king during the Hundred Years War.

At seventeen, Joan convinced the future King Charles the Seventh to give her armor and send her with an army to Orleans. The city had been under siege for months, and she helped free it in just nine days.

Joan was captured, tried by a church court backed by the English, and burned at the stake in Rouen in fourteen thirty one. She was only nineteen. Twenty five years later, a new trial declared her innocent.
Almost five hundred years after her death, in nineteen twenty, the Catholic Church declared Joan of Arc a saint. Today she is one of the patron saints of France.

hook.en: Joan of Arc was only nineteen when she died.

paintings: Ingres Joan of Arc coronation Charles VII

en: The Book of Enoch is an ancient Jewish text named after Enoch, the great grandfather of Noah. Parts of it are more than two thousand years old, and it was popular among Jews and early Christians.
The Letter of Jude, in the New Testament, actually quotes the Book of Enoch, about the Lord coming with thousands of his holy ones. Yet most churches later decided to leave Enoch out of their Bible.

For centuries, the full book was lost in Europe. But the Ethiopian Orthodox Church kept it in its Bible all along, and in the seventeen hundreds, the Scottish explorer James Bruce brought copies back from Ethiopia.

Enoch describes fallen angels called Watchers, who came down to earth and taught humans secrets like metalworking and makeup. Their children were giants, and the book says their evil led to the great flood.

hook.en: One Bible still includes the Book of Enoch.

en: During a long drought, Elijah hid by a brook, and the Bible says ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and evening. Later, a poor widow shared her last flour with him, and her jar never ran empty.

On Mount Carmel, Elijah challenged four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal to see whose god would send fire. Baal's prophets shouted all day, while Elijah even soaked his altar with water before praying.
Elijah did not die like everyone else. The Second Book of Kings says a chariot of fire and horses of fire appeared, and he was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind while his disciple Elisha watched.
Because he never died, Jewish tradition expects Elijah to return one day. At the Passover meal, many families pour a cup of wine for him and open the door, in case Elijah comes in.

hook.en: According to the Bible, Elijah never died.

en: The Holy Grail is said to be the cup Jesus used at the Last Supper. The Gospels mention the cup but never say what happened to it, and the Grail legend only appeared more than eleven hundred years later.

The first known Grail story was written in France around eleven ninety by the poet Chretien de Troyes. Surprisingly, his grail was not the cup of Jesus at all, just a mysterious dish carried through a castle.
The most famous claim is in Valencia Cathedral in Spain, an ancient agate cup that popes have even used to celebrate Mass. In Leon, also in Spain, a basilica displays another candidate.

In later legends, Joseph of Arimathea used the Grail to catch the blood of Jesus at the cross, then carried it to Britain. That is how the Grail became part of the stories of King Arthur and his knights.

hook.en: Several churches claim to have the Holy Grail.

en: Peter's real name was Simon. Jesus gave him a new name, Cephas in Aramaic and Petros in Greek, both meaning rock. That is why Jesus says, on this rock I will build my church.
Peter was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, working with his brother Andrew. He was also married, because the Gospels say Jesus healed his mother in law, who was sick with a fever.

Christian tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome under the emperor Nero. Feeling unworthy to die like Jesus, he asked to be crucified upside down. Saint Peter's Basilica stands over his traditional grave.
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing him three times before the rooster crowed. Later the risen Jesus asked him three times, do you love me, as if to undo each denial.

hook.en: Peter asked to be crucified upside down.

en: According to the Book of Joshua, the Israelites did not attack Jericho at first. They marched around the city once a day for six days, with priests blowing trumpets made of rams' horns.
On the seventh day, they marched around the city seven times. Then the priests blew the trumpets, the people gave a great shout, and the Bible says the walls of Jericho fell down flat.

Jericho is one of the oldest cities in the world. Archaeologists found a stone wall and a stone tower there more than ten thousand years old, built before writing, before metal tools, even before pottery.
Before the attack, a woman named Rahab hid two Israelite spies on her roof under stalks of flax. She tied a scarlet cord in her window as a sign, and her family was spared when the city fell.

hook.en: Jericho may be the oldest walled city on Earth.

en: The Sagrada Familia is a basilica in Barcelona, Spain, designed by the architect Antoni Gaudi. He took over the project in eighteen eighty three and spent the rest of his life working on it.
Gaudi was inspired by nature. Inside, the columns branch out like trees, so visitors feel they are standing in a stone forest, with colored light pouring in through the stained glass windows.
Building began in eighteen eighty two, and it is still not completely finished. When people asked why it was taking so long, Gaudi reportedly answered, my client is not in a hurry, meaning God.
In nineteen twenty six, Gaudi was hit by a tram in Barcelona. Dressed so simply, he was mistaken for a beggar and not treated quickly. He died days later and is buried inside his basilica.

hook.en: Construction started in eighteen eighty two, and continues today.

en: Goliath was the champion of the Philistines, from the city of Gath. For forty days, morning and evening, he came out and challenged the army of Israel to send one man to fight him.
His armor was enormous. The Bible says his bronze coat weighed five thousand shekels, about fifty seven kilograms, and the iron tip of his spear alone weighed around seven kilograms.

Most Bibles say Goliath was six cubits and a span, nearly three meters tall. But the oldest Greek translation and a Dead Sea Scroll say four cubits and a span, about two meters. Very tall, but not a monster.
David refused King Saul's armor because he was not used to it. He went out with only his staff, a sling and five smooth stones from a stream. He needed just one.

hook.en: Goliath's height depends on which Bible you read.

en: Gabriel is one of only a few angels named in the Bible. He first appears in the Book of Daniel, explaining Daniel's visions, and his name is often translated as God is my strength.
Gabriel is best known for the Annunciation. In the Gospel of Luke, he visits Mary in Nazareth and tells her she will give birth to a son, who will be called the Son of God.

Before visiting Mary, Gabriel appeared to an old priest named Zechariah to announce the birth of his son, John the Baptist. Zechariah doubted it, so Gabriel made him unable to speak until the baby was born.
Gabriel is important in Islam too. Muslims believe the angel Gabriel, Jibril in Arabic, revealed the Quran to the Prophet Muhammad. So the same angel is honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims.

hook.en: Gabriel made a priest mute for doubting him.

en: Daniel was taken from Jerusalem to Babylon as a young man. He and his friends refused the king's rich food and wine and ate only vegetables and water, yet after ten days they looked healthier than everyone else.
King Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a huge statue with a head of gold, a chest of silver, a belly of bronze, and feet of iron mixed with clay. Only Daniel could explain what it meant.

Daniel served the kings of Babylon, then kept serving when the Persians took over, under Darius and Cyrus. That is why he was still a top official when jealous rivals tricked the king into throwing him to the lions.
In the city of Susa, in modern Iran, a building with a cone shaped dome is visited as the tomb of Daniel. Other places also claim his grave, but this one has been honored for many centuries.

hook.en: Daniel served kings of two different empires.

paintings: Rubens Daniel in the Lions' Den
Briton Riviere Daniel's Answer to the King

en: The King James Bible was first published in sixteen eleven, ordered by King James the First of England. About fifty scholars worked on it in six teams, in Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge.
It gave English many everyday phrases, like a labor of love, the powers that be, the salt of the earth, and by the skin of my teeth. Many people use them without knowing they come from the Bible.

In sixteen thirty one, printers made a terrible mistake. One edition left out the word not in the Ten Commandments, so it read, thou shalt commit adultery. It became known as the Wicked Bible, and the printers were heavily fined.
More than four hundred years later, the King James Bible is still one of the best selling books in history, and many churches and readers, especially in the United States, still prefer it.

hook.en: One famous misprint told readers to commit adultery.

paintings: King James I of England portrait

en: Mount Sinai is where, according to Exodus, Moses received the Ten Commandments. The Bible says the mountain was covered in smoke and shook violently, with thunder, lightning and a very loud trumpet sound.
Moses stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights. When he came down, the Bible says his face was shining so brightly that people were afraid, so he covered it with a veil.

The Bible never clearly says where Sinai is. Since the fourth century, Christians have honored Jebel Musa in Egypt's Sinai desert, but scholars have suggested more than a dozen other mountains, some even in Saudi Arabia.

Many visitors climb Jebel Musa at night to watch the sunrise from the top. One path, called the Steps of Repentance, has about three thousand seven hundred and fifty stone steps cut by monks long ago.

hook.en: Nobody knows for sure where Mount Sinai is.

paintings: Moses receiving the Ten Commandments painting

en: Sodom and Gomorrah were cities in the plain near the Dead Sea. Genesis says Abraham bargained with God to spare Sodom, going down from fifty righteous people to just ten, but not even ten were found.
Two angels came to Sodom and warned Lot to flee with his family. Genesis says the Lord then rained down fire and burning sulfur on the cities, and smoke rose from the land like a furnace.

The angels told Lot's family not to look back, but Lot's wife did, and she became a pillar of salt. Near the Dead Sea, on a mountain made of salt called Mount Sodom, a tall rock pillar is nicknamed Lot's Wife.

Some researchers think a city near the Dead Sea, Tall el Hammam, was destroyed by an exploding space rock over three thousand five hundred years ago, and linked it to Sodom. Many other scientists strongly dispute this.

hook.en: A Dead Sea salt rock is called Lot's Wife.

paintings: John Martin Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

en: The Bible says the Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's wisdom and came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions. She arrived with a great caravan of camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones.
Nobody is sure where Sheba was. Many scholars place it in Yemen, in southern Arabia, while Ethiopian tradition places it in Ethiopia. The Bible never even gives the queen's name.

An Ethiopian holy book, the Kebra Nagast, says the queen had a son with Solomon, named Menelik. Ethiopia's emperors claimed to descend from him, right up to the last emperor, Haile Selassie, removed in nineteen seventy four.
In the Ethiopian story, Menelik later visited Solomon and brought the Ark of the Covenant back to Ethiopia. That is why the Ethiopian church says the Ark is still kept in the city of Aksum today.

hook.en: Ethiopia's emperors claimed to descend from her.

paintings: Poynter Visit of the Queen of Sheba
Piero della Francesca Queen of Sheba

en: Vatican City became an independent country in nineteen twenty nine, through an agreement between the pope and Italy. It has its own flag, stamps, coins, radio station and even its own railway station.

The Vatican Apostolic Archive holds documents from more than twelve centuries, on about eighty five kilometers of shelves. It was long called the secret archive, but the old word for secret simply meant private.
At only about forty four hectares, the Vatican is the smallest country in the world. You could walk across it in about twenty minutes, and it has only a few hundred citizens.
The Vatican has a cash machine with instructions in Latin, still an official language of the Holy See. It even has its own football league, with teams of priests, guards and museum staff.

hook.en: The Vatican is the smallest country in the world.

en: John was a relative of Jesus, born only about six months before him. Luke says that when Mary, pregnant with Jesus, visited John's mother Elizabeth, the unborn John leaped in her womb.
John baptized people in the Jordan River, calling them to change their lives. When Jesus came to be baptized, John at first refused, saying he was the one who needed to be baptized by Jesus.

John lived in the wilderness and wore clothes of camel's hair with a leather belt. Mark says he ate locusts and wild honey. Locusts are still eaten in some parts of the world, and they are full of protein.
John criticized King Herod Antipas for marrying his brother's wife. At a party, her daughter danced for Herod and, urged by her mother, asked for John's head on a platter. Herod gave the order.

hook.en: John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey.

en: The Leviathan is a sea monster mentioned several times in the Bible, in Job, the Psalms and Isaiah. Isaiah calls it the gliding serpent, the coiling serpent, the monster of the sea.
Similar monsters appear in older stories of the region. In texts from the ancient city of Ugarit, a seven headed sea serpent called Lotan fights the gods, and many scholars link it to the Leviathan.
In the Book of Job, God describes the Leviathan for a whole chapter. Smoke pours from its nostrils, flames from its mouth, its back is like rows of shields, and nothing on earth is its equal.
In sixteen fifty one, the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes named his famous book about government Leviathan. He compared a powerful state to a giant monster made of all its citizens together.

hook.en: God spends a whole chapter describing one sea monster.

en: Amen means truly, or so be it. Christians say it at the end of a prayer to agree with it and make it their own. In the Old Testament, the whole people sometimes answered amen together after a blessing.
Jesus used amen in a surprising way. He often said it at the start of a sentence, not the end, as in truly, truly, I say to you. In Greek, that is literally amen, amen.
Amen comes from a Hebrew root linked to being firm and trustworthy. It was kept untranslated in Greek, Latin and many later languages, so Jews, Christians and Muslims all still say it today.
In the Book of Revelation, Jesus himself is called the Amen, the faithful and true witness. And in many translations, amen is the very last word of the whole Bible.

hook.en: Amen is a Hebrew word used all over the world.

en: Esther was a young Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai in Susa, a capital of Persia. When King Xerxes searched for a new queen, she was chosen, but she kept her Jewish identity secret.
Before meeting the king, the young women went through twelve months of beauty treatments, the Book of Esther says, six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and cosmetics.

The Hebrew Book of Esther never mentions God, not even once. Yet it tells how Esther risked her life to save her people from a plot to destroy them, and many readers see God working quietly behind the scenes.
Jews celebrate Esther's story every year at the festival of Purim. When the book is read aloud and the villain Haman's name is spoken, people use rattles and noise to drown it out.

hook.en: God is never mentioned in the Book of Esther.

en: The Pontifical Swiss Guard has protected the pope since fifteen oh six, making it one of the oldest active military units in the world. Every guard must be a Swiss Catholic man.

On the sixth of May, fifteen twenty seven, the army of Emperor Charles the Fifth attacked Rome. One hundred and forty seven Swiss Guards died defending the pope, who escaped with only forty two survivors.

Many people say Michelangelo designed the colorful blue, red and yellow uniform, but that is a legend. The modern uniform was designed in the early nineteen hundreds by a commander of the guard, inspired by Renaissance paintings.
New guards are sworn in every year on the sixth of May, the anniversary of that battle. Each one raises three fingers, for the Holy Trinity, and swears to give his life for the pope if needed.

hook.en: Michelangelo did not design the Swiss Guard uniform.

en: Jesus grew up in Nazareth, in Galilee, which is why he was called Jesus of Nazareth. Today it is the largest Arab city in Israel, but in his time it was a tiny farming village.
In the Gospel of John, when Nathanael hears that Jesus comes from Nazareth, he asks, can anything good come from Nazareth? The village clearly did not have a great reputation.
Nazareth is never mentioned in the Old Testament, nor by the Jewish historian Josephus. It was so small that some once doubted it existed, until archaeologists found houses from the time of Jesus.

Nazareth is home to the Basilica of the Annunciation, built where tradition says the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary. Finished in nineteen sixty nine, it is often called the largest church in the Middle East.

hook.en: Nazareth is never mentioned in the Old Testament.

en: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess, the daughter of the king of Sidon, who married King Ahab of Israel. She promoted the worship of Baal and, according to the Bible, had many prophets of God killed.
When Ahab wanted a vineyard owned by a man named Naboth, who refused to sell it, Jezebel arranged false witnesses to accuse him. Naboth was stoned to death, and Ahab took the vineyard.

When the new king Jehu came to kill her, Jezebel painted her eyes, did her hair, and looked out of her window. Some see vanity, others a queen facing death with dignity. She was thrown from that window.
In nineteen sixty four, an ancient seal engraved with the name Jezebel was found. Some scholars think it may have belonged to the queen herself, while others say the name was too common to be sure.

hook.en: Jezebel did her hair just before she died.

en: The Annunciation is the moment, in the Gospel of Luke, when the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive a son. Mary's first answer is a practical question: how can this be, since I am a virgin?
Mary's reply, let it be to me according to your word, is called her fiat, from the Latin for let it be. Christians see it as one of the greatest acts of trust in the whole Bible.

The Annunciation is celebrated on the twenty fifth of March, exactly nine months before Christmas. For centuries, the twenty fifth of March was also New Year's Day in England, until seventeen fifty two.
It is one of the most painted scenes in Western art. Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico and Botticelli all painted it, often with a white lily, a symbol of Mary's purity, in the angel's hand.

hook.en: The Annunciation is exactly nine months before Christmas.

en: Mount Ararat is a huge snow capped volcano in eastern Turkey, more than five thousand one hundred meters high. It is the highest mountain in Turkey and can be seen from far away in Armenia.
Ararat is a national symbol of Armenia and appears on its coat of arms, even though the mountain is in Turkey. On clear days, it towers over the Armenian capital, Yerevan.

Genesis says the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat, not on one mountain. Ararat was the Hebrew name of an ancient kingdom called Urartu, which covered a large region. The famous peak got its name later.
Many expeditions have searched Mount Ararat for the remains of the ark. In nineteen fifty nine, aerial photos showed a boat shaped formation nearby, but geologists say it is a natural rock formation.

hook.en: The Bible never says the ark landed on Mount Ararat.

en: Advent comes from the Latin word adventus, which means coming or arrival. It is the season of waiting before Christmas, and it begins on the fourth Sunday before Christmas Day.
Advent is also the start of the Christian year. For many churches, the new church calendar begins on the first Sunday of Advent, not on the first of January.
In the Middle Ages, Advent was a time of fasting, a bit like Lent. In parts of Europe it started on the eleventh of November, the feast of Saint Martin, so it was even called Saint Martin's Lent.

The first Advent calendars appeared in Germany in the eighteen hundreds. Families drew chalk lines on a door or lit a candle each day. Printed calendars with little doors came in the early nineteen hundreds.

hook.en: Advent was once a time of fasting, like Lent.

en: In the Book of Revelation, Michael leads the angels in a war in heaven against a great dragon, identified as the devil. The dragon is defeated and thrown down to the earth.

The short Letter of Jude mentions a strange scene: Michael arguing with the devil over the body of Moses. The Bible gives no more details, and the story seems to come from an older Jewish text that is now lost.
Many angels appear in the Bible, but the word archangel is used for only one named angel, Michael. His name is a question in Hebrew, who is like God? It is a challenge, because the answer is no one.
Mont Saint-Michel in France is named after him. Legend says that in the year seven hundred and eight, Michael appeared to a local bishop and asked for a church to be built on the rocky island.

hook.en: Michael is the only angel the Bible calls an archangel.

en: An Advent wreath is a circle of evergreen branches with four candles, one lit on each Sunday of Advent. The circle, with no beginning and no end, is often seen as a symbol of eternal life.
In many traditions, three candles are purple and one is pink. The pink one is lit on the third Sunday, called Gaudete Sunday, from a Latin word meaning rejoice, because Christmas is getting close.

The Advent wreath was invented in eighteen thirty nine by Johann Hinrich Wichern, a German pastor who ran a home for poor children. The children kept asking when Christmas would come, so he put candles on an old cartwheel.
Wichern's wheel had a small candle for each weekday and a big one for each Sunday, so the children could count down every single day. Later, families kept only the four big Sunday candles.

hook.en: The first Advent wreath was made from a cartwheel.

en: Lazarus lived in Bethany, near Jerusalem, with his sisters Martha and Mary, close friends of Jesus. When Lazarus fell sick, the sisters sent for Jesus, but he waited two more days before coming.
When Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days. Jesus wept, which is the shortest verse in many English Bibles. Then he called, Lazarus, come out, and the dead man walked out.
The Gospel of John says that after this miracle, many people began to believe in Jesus. So the chief priests made plans to kill not only Jesus, but Lazarus too, the living proof of the miracle.
An old tradition says Lazarus later went to Cyprus and became the first bishop of Kition, today's Larnaca. A church there named after him stands over a tomb that tradition says is his.

hook.en: Some wanted Lazarus dead again after he came back.

paintings: Sebastiano del Piombo Raising of Lazarus

en: The Bible begins with the words, in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. God creates the world in six days, and rests on the seventh, the origin of the weekly day of rest.
On the first day God creates light, but the sun, moon and stars only appear on the fourth day. Readers, ancient and modern, have offered many explanations for this surprising order.

Genesis has two creation accounts side by side. In the first, humans are created last, after the animals. In the second, starting in chapter two, man is formed from dust first, then the garden, the animals, and finally woman.

In the sixteen hundreds, Archbishop James Ussher calculated from the Bible that creation happened in four thousand and four before Christ, on an evening in October. His date was printed in many English Bibles for centuries.

hook.en: Genesis actually begins with two creation stories.

paintings: Michelangelo Separation of Light from Darkness
Michelangelo Creation of the Sun and Moon

en: Saint Nicholas was a real bishop who lived in the three hundreds in Myra, in what is now Turkey. Stories of his kindness and secret gifts slowly turned him into Santa Claus.

The most famous legend says a poor man could not pay for his three daughters to marry. At night, Nicholas secretly threw bags of gold through their window, and in some versions, one landed in a stocking.

In ten eighty seven, sailors from Bari, Italy, took most of his bones from Myra to their city. Since then, a clear liquid called manna collects in his tomb, and every year it is gathered and shared with pilgrims.
In twenty seventeen, Oxford researchers carbon dated a bone fragment said to belong to Saint Nicholas. The result pointed to the fourth century, the time he lived, so the relic could be genuine.

hook.en: Saint Nicholas's bones give off a mysterious liquid.

paintings: Gentile da Fabriano Saint Nicholas dowry
